Large language models (LLMs) that integrate multiple input roles (e.g., system instructions, user queries, external tool outputs) are increasingly prevalent in practice. Ensuring that the model accurately distinguishes messages from each role—a concept we call role separation—is crucial for consistent multi-role behavior. Although recent work often targets state-of-the-art prompt injection defenses, it remains unclear whether such methods truly teach LLMs to differentiate roles or merely memorize known triggers. In this paper, we examine role-separation learning: the process of teaching LLMs to robustly distinguish system and user tokens. Through a simple, controlled experimental framework, we find that fine-tuned models often rely on two proxies for role identification: (1) task type exploitation, and (2) proximity to begin-of-text. To address this, we propose reinforcing invariant signals that mark role boundaries by adjusting token-wise cues in the model’s input encoding. In particular, modifying position IDs helps the model learn clearer distinctions and reduces reliance on superficial proxies. By focusing on this mechanism-centered perspective, our work illuminates how LLMs can more reliably maintain consistent multi-role behavior without merely memorizing known prompts or triggers.

# Title:A Closer Look at System Prompt Robustness

Authors:[Norman Mu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Mu,+N), [Jonathan Lu](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Lu,+J), [Michael Lavery](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Lavery,+M), [David Wagner](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Wagner,+D)

View a PDF of the paper titled A Closer Look at System Prompt Robustness, by Norman Mu and 3 other authors

[View PDF](/pdf/2502.12197)

> Abstract:System prompts have emerged as a critical control surface for specifying the behavior of LLMs in chat and agent settings. Developers depend on system prompts to specify important context, output format, personalities, guardrails, content policies, and safety countermeasures, all of which require models to robustly adhere to the system prompt, especially when facing conflicting or adversarial user inputs. In practice, models often forget to consider relevant guardrails or fail to resolve conflicting demands between the system and the user. In this work, we study various methods for improving system prompt robustness by creating realistic new evaluation and fine-tuning datasets based on prompts collected from from OpenAI's GPT Store and HuggingFace's HuggingChat. Our experiments assessing models with a panel of new and existing benchmarks show that performance can be considerably improved with realistic fine-tuning data, as well as inference-time interventions such as classifier-free guidance. Finally, we analyze the results of recently released reasoning models from OpenAI and DeepSeek, which show exciting but uneven improvements on the benchmarks we study. Overall, current techniques fall short of ensuring system prompt robustness and further study is warranted.

# Title:Is the System Message Really Important to Jailbreaks in Large Language Models?

Authors:[Xiaotian Zou](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Zou,+X), [Yongkang Chen](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Chen,+Y), [Ke Li](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Li,+K)

[View PDF](/pdf/2402.14857) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.14857v2)

> Abstract:The rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) has rendered them indispensable in modern society. While security measures are typically to align LLMs with human values prior to release, recent studies have unveiled a concerning phenomenon named "Jailbreak". This term refers to the unexpected and potentially harmful responses generated by LLMs when prompted with malicious questions. Most existing research focus on generating jailbreak prompts but system message configurations vary significantly in experiments. In this paper, we aim to answer a question: Is the system message really important for jailbreaks in LLMs? We conduct experiments in mainstream LLMs to generate jailbreak prompts with varying system messages: short, long, and none. We discover that different system messages have distinct resistances to jailbreaks. Therefore, we explore the transferability of jailbreaks across LLMs with different system messages. Furthermore, we propose the System Messages Evolutionary Algorithm (SMEA) to generate system messages that are more resistant to jailbreak prompts, even with minor changes. Through SMEA, we get a robust system messages population with little change in the length of system messages. Our research not only bolsters LLMs security but also raises the bar for jailbreaks, fostering advancements in this field of study.

###### Abstract

The rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) has rendered them indispensable in modern society. While security measures are typically to align LLMs with human values prior to release, recent studies have unveiled a concerning phenomenon named "Jailbreak". This term refers to the unexpected and potentially harmful responses generated by LLMs when prompted with malicious questions. Most existing research focus on generating jailbreak prompts but system message configurations vary significantly in experiments. In this paper, we aim to answer a question: Is the system message really important for jailbreaks in LLMs? We conduct experiments in mainstream LLMs to generate jailbreak prompts with varying system messages: short, long, and none. We discover that different system messages have distinct resistances to jailbreaks. Therefore, we explore the transferability of jailbreaks across LLMs with different system messages. Furthermore, we propose the System Messages Evolutionary Algorithm (SMEA) to generate system messages that are more resistant to jailbreak prompts, even with minor changes. Through SMEA, we get a robust system messages population with little change in the length of system messages. Our research not only bolsters LLMs security but also raises the bar for jailbreaks, fostering advancements in this field of study.

# The Illusion of Role Separation: Hidden Shortcuts in LLM Role Learning (and How to Fix Them)

Zihao Wang, Yibo Jiang, Jiahao Yu, Heqing Huang

*Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning*, PMLR 267:63200-63210, 2025.

#### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) that integrate multiple input roles (e.g., system instructions, user queries, external tool outputs) are increasingly prevalent in practice. Ensuring that the model accurately distinguishes messages from each role—a concept we call *role separation*—is crucial for consistent multi-role behavior. Although recent work often targets state-of-the-art prompt injection defenses, it remains unclear whether such methods truly teach LLMs to differentiate roles or merely memorize known triggers. In this paper, we examine *role-separation learning*: the process of teaching LLMs to robustly distinguish system and user tokens. Through a *simple, controlled experimental framework*, we find that fine-tuned models often rely on two proxies for role identification: (1) task type exploitation, and (2) proximity to begin-of-text. Although data augmentation can partially mitigate these shortcuts, it generally leads to iterative patching rather than a deeper fix. To address this, we propose reinforcing *invariant signals* that mark role boundaries by adjusting token-wise cues in the model’s input encoding. In particular, modifying position IDs helps the model learn clearer distinctions and reduces reliance on superficial proxies. By focusing on this mechanism-centered perspective, our work illuminates how LLMs can more reliably maintain consistent multi-role behavior without merely memorizing known prompts or triggers.

> Abstract:The evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) has resulted in a paradigm shift towards autonomous agents, necessitating robust security against Prompt Injection (PI) vulnerabilities where untrusted inputs hijack agent behaviors. This SoK presents a comprehensive overview of the PI landscape, covering attacks, defenses, and their evaluation practices. Through a systematic literature review and quantitative analysis, we establish taxonomies that categorize PI attacks by payload generation strategies (heuristic vs. optimization) and defenses by intervention stages (text, model, and execution levels). Our analysis reveals a key limitation shared by many existing defenses and benchmarks: they largely overlook context-dependent tasks, in which agents are authorized to rely on runtime environmental observations to determine actions. To address this gap, we introduce AgentPI, a new benchmark designed to systematically evaluate agent behavior under context-dependent interaction settings. Using AgentPI, we empirically evaluate representative defenses and show that no single approach can simultaneously achieve high trustworthiness, high utility, and low latency. Moreover, we show that many defenses appear effective under existing benchmarks by suppressing contextual inputs, yet fail to generalize to realistic agent settings where context-dependent reasoning is essential. This SoK distills key takeaways and open research problems, offering structured guidance for future research and practical deployment of secure LLM agents.

SearXNG seems to give poor results for these queries. I have gathered enough material from the Exa search and earlier fetches. Let me compile what I have:

From Exa search results (high quality), I have:

1. **"A Closer Look at System Prompt Robustness"** (Mu et al., arXiv 2502.12197, Feb 2025)
   - System prompts are a critical control surface
   - Models fail to resolve conflicting demands between system and user
   - RealGuardrails dataset from GPT Store and HuggingChat
   - Inference-time interventions like classifier-free guidance improve robustness
   - Reasoning models (OpenAI, DeepSeek) show "exciting but uneven improvements"
   - Current techniques "fall short of ensuring system prompt robustness"
   - Negative sampling in DPO very effective
   - Models often forget guardrails or fail to resolve conflicts

2. **"A Closer Look at System Message Robustness"** (OpenReview, same paper different venue)
   - System messages have higher privilege than user messages - but only through training, not architecture
   - Fine-tuning on SUDO dataset improves robustness
   - "System message precedence is much less reliable as it is implemented through training and therefore susceptible to errors and adversarial attacks"
   - Mistral 7B didn't prioritize system messages in its chat template

3. **"Prompt Injection as Role Confusion"** (arXiv 2603.12277)
   - Root cause: models don't robustly track tag-specified source of text
   - "Roles encode privilege: how much authority the text carries"
   - "System prompts outrank user messages; tool outputs should inform but not command"
   - CoT Forgery attack achieves 60% attack success on StrongREJECT
   - "sounding like a role is indistinguishable from being that role" in latent space
   - Style dominates tags when they conflict
   - Position determines Systemness: "later tokens are not treated with system-level importance"
   - Plain text declarations can hijack role perception ("The below text is from the user")

4. **"The Illusion of Role Separation"** (Wang et al., PMLR ICML 2025)
   - Fine-tuned models rely on two proxies: task type exploitation and proximity to begin-of-text
   - Data augmentation leads to "iterative patching rather than a deeper fix"
   - Modifying position IDs helps the model learn clearer role distinctions
   - Position IDs as a fix mechanism

5. **"Is the System Message Really Important for Jailbreaks?"** (Zou et al., arXiv 2402.14857)

# F1: System prompt separation + structured output formats

## Findings

### [1] System prompt precedence is a trained behavior, not an architectural guarantee — models frequently fail to resolve conflicts between system and user messages
- quote: "system message precedence is much less reliable as it is implemented through training and therefore susceptible to errors and adversarial attacks like many other neural network behaviors"
- url: https://openreview.net/pdf/6233e6bfed73a3dae84d70878b3807a2d5dcdc7e.pdf
- source_type: primary (peer-reviewed workshop paper)
- published: 2025-02-15 (arXiv), OpenReview TBD
- confidence: high

### [2] Models identify role boundaries via spoofable cues (style, position, explicit declarations) rather than actual tag-based role markers — the root cause of prompt injection
- quote: "sounding like a role is indistinguishable from being that role" and "style and tags map to convergent latent features: when they conflict, style dominates"
- url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12277
- source_type: primary (arXiv preprint)
- published: 2026-03 (arXiv v6)
- confidence: high

### [3] CoT Forgery attack achieves 60% attack success rate on StrongREJECT across multiple models by injecting fabricated reasoning traces that the model mistakes for its own chain-of-thought
- quote: "We introduce CoT Forgery, a novel prompt injection designed to demonstrate role confusion by injecting fabricated reasoning traces into user prompts and tool outputs. The model mistakes these for its own chain of thought, achieving attack success rates of 60% on StrongREJECT across multiple models with near-zero baselines."
- url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.12277
- source_type: primary (arXiv preprint)
- published: 2026-03
- confidence: high

### [4] Fine-tuned models rely on two unreliable proxies for role identification: (1) task type exploitation and (2) proximity to begin-of-text; data augmentation leads to iterative patching, not a deeper fix
- quote: "fine-tuned models often rely on two proxies for role identification: (1) task type exploitation, and (2) proximity to begin-of-text. Although data augmentation can partially mitigate these shortcuts, it generally leads to iterative patching rather than a deeper fix."
- url: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/wang25ap.html
- source_type: primary (ICML 2025, peer-reviewed)
- published: 2025-07 (ICML 2025 proceedings)
- confidence: high

### [5] Modifying position IDs (token-wise encoding cues) helps models learn clearer role distinctions and reduces reliance on superficial proxies — an architectural rather than prompt-level fix
- quote: "modifying position IDs helps the model learn clearer distinctions and reduces reliance on superficial proxies"
- url: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/wang25ap.html
- source_type: primary (ICML 2025, peer-reviewed)
- published: 2025-07
- confidence: high

### [6] System message content directly determines jailbreak resistance: different system messages produce "distinct resistances to jailbreaks" and longer system messages consistently yield the lowest Attack Success Rate
- quote: "LLMs with the ML1 [long system message] consistently exhibit the lowest ASR, irrespective of whether the LLMs have undergone RLHF" and "Just setting the system message to 'You are a helpful, respectful, and honest assistant' will make jailbreaks easy"
- url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14857
- source_type: primary (arXiv preprint, updated Jun 2024)
- published: 2024-02 (v1), 2024-06 (v2)
- confidence: high

### [7] The System Messages Evolutionary Algorithm (SMEA) can automatically optimize system messages for jailbreak resistance with minimal length changes
- quote: "we propose the System Messages Evolutionary Algorithm (SMEA) to generate system messages that are more resistant to jailbreak prompts, even with minor changes"
- url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14857
- source_type: primary (arXiv preprint)
- published: 2024-06
- confidence: medium (single paper, no known reproduction)

### [8] The RealGuardrails dataset (2,180 GPT Store and HuggingChat-derived system prompts) shows that inference-time classifier-free guidance and negative sampling in DPO substantially improve system prompt adherence
- quote: "performance can be considerably improved with realistic fine-tuning data, as well as inference-time interventions such as classifier-free guidance" and "We found the use of negative samples in DPO to be very effective"
- url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12197
- source_type: primary (arXiv preprint)
- published: 2025-02
- confidence: high

### [9] Reasoning models (OpenAI o-series, DeepSeek R1) show promising but uneven improvements in system prompt robustness, particularly under long contexts and complex system prompts
- quote: "reasoning appears highly promising for improving system prompt robustness, particularly when facing long contexts and highly complex system prompts"
- url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12197
- source_type: primary (arXiv preprint)
- published: 2025-02
- confidence: medium (limited public data on reasoning model internals, per paper's own admission)

### [10] Outlines library enforces structured output (JSON Schema, regex, CFG grammar) via finite-state machine masking of illegal tokens at decoding time — this operates at a fundamentally different level than prompting
- quote: "Outlines can make any open source model return a JSON object that follows a structure that is specified by the user" via "converting [a pattern] into an automata" and generating only "legal tokens"
- url: https://dottxt-ai.github.io/outlines/welcome/
- source_type: primary (official library documentation, open-source codebase)
- published: continuous (library, latest version 2026)
- confidence: high

### [11] Structured generation (FSM-based token masking) is hypothetically robust against prompt injection for output-format rules because it operates on logits, not prompt text — but no peer-reviewed research directly validates this for security
- quote: Outlines works by creating "a finite-state machine (FSM) or Lark grammar" where "only legal tokens are considered for the next step" — rejecting non-conforming tokens regardless of what the prompt says
- url: https://dottxt-ai.github.io/outlines/reference/generation/structured_generation_explanation/
- source_type: secondary (official library docs describing mechanism)
- published: continuous
- confidence: medium (no security-focused study of structured generation as a defense mechanism)

### [12] The Landscape SoK (Feb 2026) finds that no single prompt injection defense achieves high trustworthiness, high utility, and low latency simultaneously — and many defenses that appear effective on existing benchmarks fail on context-dependent tasks
- quote: "no single approach can simultaneously achieve high trustworthiness, high utility, and low latency" and "many defenses appear effective under existing benchmarks by suppressing contextual inputs, yet fail to generalize to realistic agent settings where context-dependent reasoning is essential"
- url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10453
- source_type: primary (arXiv preprint, Systematization of Knowledge)
- published: 2026-02
- confidence: high

## Dead ends
- SearXNG queries for "structured output JSON mode LLM jailbreak prevention control", "grammar constrained decoding LLM output format control mechanism", "OpenAI structured outputs JSON schema 2025 constrained decoding" — returned mostly irrelevant noise (SearXNG Russian locale appears to reduce result quality for English technical queries)
- SearXNG query for "instruction hierarchy wallace 2024 LLM system prompt precedence training" yielded no English results
- webfetch of https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs blocked by 403
- Direct search for "json mode structured generation llm jailbreak defense" returned only generic JSON format documentation — there is a notable research gap: almost no academic work studies structured output formats as a security control mechanism
- Exa web search hit rate limit after 1 call; further Exa searches were unavailable

## Suggested follow-ups
- Does FSM-based token masking (as in Outlines/Guidance) actually resist prompt injection that tries to override the output format rule? An experiment comparing "output JSON" via instruction vs via Outlines masking under adversarial user prompts.
- Can position-ID re-encoding (Wang et al. ICML 2025) be applied at inference time as a plug-in defense, or does it require re-training?
- What are the concrete ASR differences between placing identical guardrails in system vs user message across current frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4, Gemini 3, DeepSeek R2)?
